title: A hammer and a feather on the Moon
hook: On Earth the feather drifts down last. With no air at all, does weight still win?

knows: on Earth a feather falls more slowly than a hammer
the Moon has weaker gravity and no air
doesNotKnow: that air drag causes the difference
that gravity gives every mass the same acceleration

misconception: Heavier objects fall faster because they are heavier.
objective: The learner can explain that without air every object falls with the same acceleration whatever its mass, and that air drag is what makes light, wide objects lag on Earth.

claims.text: Without air, every object falls with the same acceleration whatever its mass: a heavier object is pulled harder but is just as much harder to speed up.
claims.source: m a = m g, so a = g for any m (equivalence of gravitational and inertial mass). Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 2 and 5.

claims.text: Gravity at the Moon's surface is 1.62 m/s^2.
claims.source: NASA Goddard, Moon Fact Sheet (nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/moonfact.html): surface gravity 1.62 m/s^2.

claims.text: Released from 1.5 m on the Moon with no air, both land 1.36 s later.
claims.source: t = sqrt(2 h / g) = sqrt(3 / 1.62) = 1.361 s. The lesson integrates y'' = -g with RK4 at 1/600 s and gets 1.361 s.

claims.text: With air switched on (an imagined Moon with Earth-like air), the feather lags: it lands after about 3.9 s while the hammer still lands at about 1.36 s.
claims.source: Quadratic drag F = 1/2 rho C_d A v^2, rho = 1.2 kg/m^3, g = 1.62 m/s^2, RK4 at 1/600 s. Illustrative drag values chosen by the builder: feather k/m = 9.81 per metre (terminal speed 1 m/s in Earth air and gravity), hammer C_d A = 0.01 m^2. Results: feather 3.87 s; hammer 1.361 to 1.365 s for 5 kg to 0.5 kg.

claims.text: Air pushes back hard on something light and wide, which is why a feather lags on Earth.
claims.source: Drag deceleration is F / m = rho C_d A v^2 / (2 m): large drag area per unit mass means large deceleration (Taylor, Classical Mechanics, ch. 2).

claims.text: On the Moon in 1971, Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather and they landed together.
claims.source: NASA, Apollo 15 Lunar Surface Journal, 'The Hammer and the Feather' (hq.nasa.gov/alsj/a15/a15.clsout3.html), 2 August 1971.

recall.question: In a large vacuum chamber on Earth, a bowling ball and a feather are released together from the same height. What happens?
recall.why: Without air, gravity accelerates every mass equally; air drag is what makes a feather lag.
